claim: Subjective cognitive impairment (SCI) is a common condition describing self-reported deficits in cognition without objective evidence of cognitive impairment.
source: Subjective cognitive impairment (SCI) is a common condition describing self-reported deficits in cognition without objective evidence of cognitive impairment.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that establishes the clinical characterization of SCI based on established diagnostic criteria.

claim: Many individuals with SCI suffer from depression and anxiety.
source: Many individuals with SCI suffer from depression and anxiety, which have been hypothesised to account for their cognitive complaints.
evidence: This statement references established clinical observations about the association between SCI and affective disorders.

claim: People with SCI are hyperreactive to uncertainty.
source: Here, we show that people with SCI are hyperreactive to uncertainty and that this might be a key mechanism accounting for their affective burden.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by behavioral task data showing faster and more extensive sampling in SCI participants.

claim: SCI participants sampled faster than matched controls across different conditions.
source: Across different conditions, SCI participants sampled faster and obtained more information than matched controls to resolve uncertainty.
evidence: This claim is supported by inter-sampling interval measurements from the active information gathering task.

claim: SCI participants obtained more information than matched controls.
source: Across different conditions, SCI participants sampled faster and obtained more information than matched controls to resolve uncertainty.
evidence: This is supported by the number of samples acquired by SCI participants compared to controls in the behavioral task.

claim: Despite their 'urgent' sampling behaviour, SCI participants were able to maintain their efficiency.
source: Remarkably, despite their 'urgent' sampling behaviour, SCI participants were able to maintain their efficiency.
evidence: This is supported by the information extraction rate (α) measurements showing no significant difference between groups.

claim: Hyperreactivity to uncertainty indexed by sampling behaviour correlated with the severity of affective burden including depression and anxiety.
source: Hyperreactivity to uncertainty indexed by this sampling behaviour correlated with the severity of affective burden including depression and anxiety.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses between sampling speed/over-sampling and affective burden scores.

claim: SCI participants had stronger insular-hippocampal connectivity compared to controls.
source: Analysis of MRI resting functional connectivity revealed that SCI participants had stronger insular-hippocampal connectivity compared to controls, which also correlated with faster sampling.
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain ROI-to-ROI functional connectivity analysis from resting-state fMRI data.

claim: Stronger insular-hippocampal connectivity correlated with faster sampling in SCI.
source: Analysis of MRI resting functional connectivity revealed that SCI participants had stronger insular-hippocampal connectivity compared to controls, which also correlated with faster sampling.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between connectivity strength and inter-sampling interval.

claim: Altered uncertainty processing is a key mechanism underlying the psycho-cognitive manifestations in SCI.
source: These results suggest that altered uncertainty processing is a key mechanism underlying the psycho-cognitive manifestations in SCI and implicate a specific brain network target for future treatment.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the behavioral and neuroimaging findings of the study.

claim: An increasing number of people are seeking medical advice for concerns about cognitive decline with an ageing population.
source: With an ageing population, an increasing number of people are seeking medical advice for concerns about cognitive decline (Deary et al., 2009; Harada et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by cited references documenting demographic trends.

claim: Cognitive complaints can be expressed by people without an underlying neurodegenerative disorder.
source: While in some individuals these complaints might be related to a progressive pathological process such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), they can also be expressed by people without an underlying neurodegenerative disorder (McWhirter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference documenting clinical observations.

claim: When objective clinical evidence of significant cognitive impairment is not evident alongside self-reported cognitive complaints, individuals are categorised as having subjective cognitive impairment/decline (SCI/D).
source: When objective clinical evidence of significant cognitive impairment is not evident alongside self-reported cognitive complaints, individuals are categorised as having subjective cognitive impairment/decline (SCI/D) (Jessen et al., 2014; Jessen et al., 2020; Reid and Maclullich, 2006).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by cited diagnostic criteria.

claim: Most individuals with SCI follow a relatively benign course.
source: Although most follow a relatively benign course, a small proportion develops objective cognitive impairment and subsequently progress to dementia (Arvanitakis et al., 2018; Kryscio et al., 2014; Mendonça et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited longitudinal studies of SCI outcomes.

claim: A small proportion of individuals with SCI develops objective cognitive impairment and subsequently progress to dementia.
source: Although most follow a relatively benign course, a small proportion develops objective cognitive impairment and subsequently progress to dementia (Arvanitakis et al., 2018; Kryscio et al., 2014; Mendonça et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited longitudinal studies documenting progression rates.

claim: There is a particularly high prevalence of mental health problems associated with SCI, in particular affective disorders such as anxiety and depression.
source: A wealth of evidence suggests a particularly high prevalence of a range of mental health problems associated with SCI, in particular affective disorders such as anxiety and depression (Hill et al., 2016; Hohman et al., 2011; Pavisic et al., 2021; Reid and Maclullich, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies documenting the association between SCI and affective disorders.

claim: People who primarily suffer from psychiatric disorders often report sub-optimal cognitive performance.
source: Similarly, people who primarily suffer from these psychiatric disorders often report sub-optimal cognitive performance, further emphasising the intertwined relationship between affective burden and subjective cognitive experience (Millan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference documenting cognitive complaints in psychiatric populations.

claim: Treating anxiety and depression may improve subjective cognitive complaints in individuals with SCI.
source: Moreover, treating anxiety and depression may improve subjective cognitive complaints in individuals with SCI (Allott et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study examining treatment effects.

claim: Affective dysregulation might be related to uncertainty processing and related behaviours.
source: A rich body of theoretical and empirical work suggests that affective dysregulation might be related to uncertainty processing and related behaviours (Bishop and Gagne, 2018; Carleton, 2016; Grupe and Nitschke, 2013; Gu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited theoretical and empirical studies.

claim: People who express higher levels of anxiety and depression often report higher levels of intolerance to uncertainty.
source: People who express higher levels of anxiety and depression often report higher levels of intolerance to uncertainty (Boelen et al., 2016; Boswell et al., 2013; Carleton et al., 2012; McEvoy and Mahoney, 2011; Saulnier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies documenting the relationship between affective symptoms and uncertainty intolerance.

claim: All participants had ACE-III cognitive scores within normal performance limits (>87/100).
source: All participants (healthy controls and individuals with SCI) had ACE-III cognitive scores within normal performance limits (>87/100) (Bruno and Schurmann Vignaga, 2019; Elamin et al., 2016; Hsieh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic of the study sample supported by standardized cognitive assessment.

claim: The affective burden dimension accounted for 84% of the variance shared between depression and anxiety.
source: This dimension could be regarded as a measure of affective burden in participants and accounted for 84% of the variance shared between depression and anxiety.
evidence: This is supported by principal component analysis of depression and anxiety scores.

claim: Extensive sampling in SCI is not related to the way individuals estimate or value uncertainty.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that extensive sampling in SCI is not related to the way individuals estimate or value uncertainty. Instead, it is likely to capture an intrinsic drive to gather information specifically when SCI have agency over the level of uncertainty (i.e. during active sampling) (see Appendix 1 for a computational model capturing this effect).
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the passive task results showing intact uncertainty estimation and valuation.

claim: Individuals with SCI exceeded the speed-efficiency trade-off that characterised healthy controls' sampling.
source: In other words, individuals with SCI exceeded the speed-efficiency trade-off that characterised healthy controls' sampling (Figure 4c.).
evidence: This is an interpretive statement supported by the combination of faster sampling and maintained efficiency in SCI.

claim: Hyperreactivity to uncertainty (indexed by faster and extensive sampling) is associated with affective dysregulation in SCI, mainly when agency is involved.
source: These results thus indicate that hyperreactivity to uncertainty (indexed by faster and extensive sampling) is associated with affective dysregulation in SCI, mainly when agency is involved.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the correlation between sampling behavior and affective burden, and the lack of group differences in the passive task.

claim: There was no other significant difference in resting functional connectivity between any of the other ROIs included in the analysis.
source: There was no other significant difference in resting functional connectivity between any of the other ROIs included in the analysis.
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain ROI-to-ROI functional connectivity analysis showing specificity of the insular-hippocampal finding.

claim: Functional connectivity disruptions in SCI participants appeared to be limited and specific to the insular-hippocampal network.
source: Thus, functional connectivity disruptions in SCI participants appeared to be limited and specific to the insular-hippocampal network highlighted in Figure 6a.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the specificity of the connectivity findings.

claim: The insular-hippocampal connectivity suggests a role for this network over-activity in the urgent information sampling behaviour exhibited by SCI participants.
source: This suggests a role for this network over-activity in the urgent information sampling behaviour exhibited by SCI participants.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the correlation between connectivity and sampling speed.

claim: The results point to a specific deficit in processing uncertainty in individuals with SCI that might be underlying their affective dysregulation.
source: Overall, the results point to a specific deficit in processing uncertainty in individuals with SCI that might be underlying their affective dysregulation and is related to increased insular-hippocampal connectivity in the condition.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating the behavioral and neuroimaging findings.

claim: The results point to a deficit in processing uncertainty that is related to increased insular-hippocampal connectivity in SCI.
source: Overall, the results point to a specific deficit in processing uncertainty in individuals with SCI that might be underlying their affective dysregulation and is related to increased insular-hippocampal connectivity in the condition.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating the behavioral and neuroimaging findings.

claim: People with depression and anxiety might have altered uncertainty processing.
source: These results resonate with previous research indicating that people with depression and anxiety might have altered uncertainty processing (Bishop and Gagne, 2018; Boswell et al., 2013; Carleton et al., 2012; Grupe and Nitschke, 2013; Gu et al., 2020; Hartley and Phelps, 2012; Pulcu and Browning, 2019; Saulnier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on uncertainty processing in affective disorders.

claim: A common factor accounting for shared variance between depression and anxiety was associated with disrupted learning in probabilistic environments reflecting impaired uncertainty processing.
source: A recent investigation, for example, showed that a common factor accounting for shared variance between both syndromes was associated with disrupted learning in probabilistic environments reflecting impaired uncertainty processing (Gagne et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on learning and uncertainty in affective disorders.

claim: Individuals suffering from depression tend to acquire more high-utility information than non-depressed individuals in a simulated interview environment.
source: One early investigation in social psychology showed that individuals suffering from depression tend to acquire more high-utility information than non-depressed individuals in a simulated interview environment where participants played the role of the interviewer and had to select interview questions from a standardised list of questions that differed in their diagnostic utility (Hildebrand-Saints and Weary, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on information gathering in depression.

claim: Previous studies using classical behavioural paradigms of information seeking such as the beads task failed to report consistent effects of anxiety and depression on performance.
source: For example, previous studies using classical behavioural paradigms of information seeking such as the beads task failed to report consistent effects of anxiety and depression on performance (Jacoby et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited review of studies using the beads task.

claim: Controllability has been hypothesised to be a crucial feature of both anxiety and depression.
source: Such inconsistencies might be due to the fact that the behavioural paradigms used in these prior studies often neglect an important aspect of information gathering – controllability – which has been hypothesised to be a crucial feature of both anxiety and depression (Abramson et al., 1978; Barlow, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by cited theoretical work on controllability in affective disorders.

claim: Acquiring more samples allowed SCI participants to achieve lower uncertainty levels prior to decisions.
source: Second, acquiring more samples indeed allowed SCI participants to achieve lower uncertainty levels prior to decisions, suggesting that these additional samples carried instrumental utility and were not merely reflective of wasteful sampling behaviour driven by insensitivity to reward.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis showing lower expected error at the end of sampling in SCI participants.

claim: SCI participants and controls might differ in the subjective cost they assign to sampling speed and efficiency.
source: Another account of SCI individuals' extensive sampling behaviour might involve subjective costs that are not directly specified in economic terms in the task. Namely, SCI individuals and controls might differ in the subjective cost they assign to sampling speed and efficiency.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: Given that SCI participants sampled faster but as efficiently as controls, subjective costs of sampling appear to be lower in this population.
source: Given that SCI participants sampled faster but as efficiently as controls, these subjective costs appear to be lower in this population (see Appendix 1 for a formal demonstration using a computational model).
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the behavioral findings and computational modeling.

claim: Various brain regions have previously been implicated in anxiety and depression including amygdala, hippocampus, and insular cortex.
source: Various brain regions have previously been implicated in anxiety and depression and their mechanistic characterisation as deficits in uncertainty processing including amygdala (Grupe and Nitschke, 2013; Morriss et al., 2019), hippocampus (Gray and McNaughton, 2003; Harrison et al., 2006; Rigoli et al., 2019; Strange et al., 2005; Tobia et al., 2012), and insular cortex (Grupe and Nitschke, 2013; Morriss et al., 2019; Tanovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on brain regions involved in affective disorders and uncertainty processing.

claim: The insular cortex receives input from different brain regions carrying interoceptive information about various bodily sensations.
source: The insular cortex receives input from different brain regions carrying interoceptive information about various bodily sensations, such as temperature, heartbeat, bowel distension and more (Namkung et al., 2017; Uddin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited reviews of insular cortex function.

claim: Subjective experience of interoceptive stimuli has been shown to correlate with insular activity on functional neuroimaging.
source: Subjective experience of these stimuli has been shown to correlate with insular activity on functional neuroimaging using MRI or positron emission tomography (Craig et al., 2000; Critchley et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited neuroimaging studies of interoception.

claim: Recent accounts of insular function extend its contribution to involve emotional states and higher subjective awareness.
source: More recent accounts of insular function extend this contribution of subjective awareness to involve emotional states and higher subjective awareness (Chang et al., 2013; Craig, 2009; Namkung et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited theoretical and empirical work on insular function.

claim: A few studies have demonstrated altered insular task-related activity in SCI linked to impaired memory performance and future-guided decision making.
source: A few studies have demonstrated altered insular task-related activity in SCI linked to impaired memory performance and future-guided decision making, however, without pointing to how these findings are related to affective burden or subjectivity (Cai et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on insular activity in SCI.

claim: Damage to the insula might impair subjectivity and self-awareness as seen in patients with anosognosia for hemiplegia and other forms of insular injury.
source: By contrast, damage to the insula might impair subjectivity and self-awareness as seen in patients with anosognosia for hemiplegia and other forms of insular injury (Fotopoulou et al., 2010; Karnath et al., 2005; Spinazzola et al., 2008), as well as resulting in dysfunctional emotional awareness (e.g. as seen in fronto-temporal dementia), under-reactivity, lack of self-monitoring and passivity (Kleiner et al., 2007; Manes et al., 1999; Sturm et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited lesion studies and clinical observations.

claim: One prominent view of hippocampal involvement in goal-directed behaviour suggests that it constitutes a crucial part of a behavioural inhibition system (BIS) that is concerned with processing aversive cues such as uncertainty.
source: One prominent view of hippocampal involvement in goal-directed behaviour suggests that it constitutes a crucial part of a behavioural inhibition system (BIS) that is concerned with processing aversive cues such as uncertainty (Gray and McNaughton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a cited theoretical framework of hippocampal function.

claim: It has been suggested that hyperactivity of the BIS might be an important neurobiological basis of anxiety and affective dysregulation.
source: It has therefore been suggested that hyperactivity of the BIS might be an important neurobiological basis of anxiety and affective dysregulation (Gray and McNaughton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a cited theoretical framework.

claim: When anticipating decisions and actions under uncertainty, the hippocampus might be encoding possible future states and their associated risks.
source: When anticipating decisions and actions under uncertainty, the hippocampus might be encoding possible future states and their associated risks (Addis et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011; Schacter et al., 2008; Schacter et al., 2017; Weiler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on hippocampal function in prospection and decision-making.

claim: Previous fMRI studies in SCI have shown altered connectivity between temporal brain regions and several other areas and networks including default mode and salience networks.
source: These neuroimaging findings are consistent with previous fMRI studies (task-related and resting) in SCI showing altered connectivity between temporal brain regions (e.g. hippocampus and para-hippocampus) and several other areas and networks including default mode and salience networks (Cai et al., 2020; Dillen et al., 2017; Hafkemeijer et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2017; Rodda et al., 2009; Verfaillie et al., 2018; Viviano and Damoiseaux, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited neuroimaging studies in SCI.

claim: The hippocampus seems to be a key region commonly involved in SCI by many fMRI studies, though a consistent pattern of its activity is still lacking.
source: While the hippocampus seems to be a key region commonly involved in SCI by many fMRI studies, a consistent pattern of its activity in the condition is still lacking (Dillen et al., 2017; Hafkemeijer et al., 2013; Rodda et al., 2009; Verfaillie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on cited neuroimaging studies showing inconsistent findings.

claim: SCI participants were clinically assessed by trained neurologists in the cognitive disorders clinic.
source: SCI participants were clinically assessed by trained neurologists (co-authors MH and SM) in the cognitive disorders clinic at John Radcliff Hospital, Oxford.
evidence: This describes the clinical assessment procedure for SCI participants.

claim: The diagnosis of SCI was supported by normal performance on standardised objective cognitive assessment using ACE-III with cutoff >87/100.
source: In addition to clinical assessment, the diagnosis of SCI was supported by normal performance on standardised objective cognitive assessment using Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination (ACE-III) with cutoff >87/100 (Bruno and Schurmann Vignaga, 2019; Elamin et al., 2016; Hsieh et al., 2013) as well as normal clinical MRI scan.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic criteria used for SCI in the study.

claim: The SCI diagnosis definition is consistent with criteria proposed in previous key reports.
source: This definition is consistent with the criteria proposed in previous key reports (Jessen et al., 2014; Jessen et al., 2020), suggesting that SCI diagnosis relies on two key components (i) subjective report of cognitive decline and (ii) normal performance on standardised objective cognitive tests.
evidence: This statement references established diagnostic criteria for SCI.

claim: Neuroimaging data were obtained from 23 SCI participants and 25 healthy controls who were MRI compatible and gave consent to be scanned.
source: All participants completed the behavioural tasks and questionnaires. Neuroimaging data were obtained from 23 SCI participants and 25 healthy controls who were MRI compatible and gave consent to be scanned for research purposes.
evidence: This describes the neuroimaging subsample of the study.

claim: Uncertainty in the task was quantified as expected error (EE) which is the average error an ideal participant would obtain by placing the localisation disc at the best possible location given the dots on the screen.
source: Uncertainty in Circle Quest paradigm was quantified as the expected error (EE), that is the average error an ideal participant would obtain by placing the localisation disc (blue disc) at the best possible location given the dots on the screen (i.e. given the information displayed).
evidence: This describes the operational definition of uncertainty used in the study.

claim: Whole-brain ROI-to-ROI analysis examined 780 connections, controlling for age and gender differences.
source: Overall, this analysis examined 780 connections, controlling for age and gender differences.
evidence: This describes the scope of the functional connectivity analysis.
